One of the approaches in the project on [speeding up first-in-human
T-cell engager studies](index.qmd). The registry and abstract search was
run on 2026-09-10. Every source is characterized from a registry record,
an abstract or a press release; none has been read, and every entry in
the
[references](references.qmd#reading-queue-t-cell-engagers-in-healthy-volunteers)
carries ❌.
:::

## In Brief

**The idea.** Give healthy volunteers (HVs) one or two doses of the
T-cell engager (TCE), climbing a dose ladder until the first sign of
activity: a grade 1 cytokine release (fever), or peripheral B cells
falling by half. That dose, found in weeks in a phase 1 unit, becomes
the starting neighbourhood for patients, and the patient study begins
where a conventional escalation would have finished.

**✅ It has been done.** Three healthy volunteer studies of TCEs are
registered, all started between December 2025 and July 2026, all in
Melbourne, all for autoimmune indications, and all subcutaneous. None
has posted a result. Section 2 has the table.

**⚠️ It applies to autoimmune programmes only.** The three sponsors that
dosed volunteers built molecules with a tuned CD3 arm and an extended
half-life, for one or two administrations, and a volunteer's B-cell
count is the same measurement as a patient's. In oncology the target
burden that drives cytokine release is absent in a volunteer, so a
volunteer's fever dose says little about a tumour patient's, and no
oncology TCE has been given to volunteers. Section 4 works through the
translation.

**It saves six months to a year** against a conventional escalation in
patients, under the assumptions in Section 5, which a programme should
replace with its own.

**❌ The Ouro question is unresolved.** A colleague recalled a Chinese
healthy volunteer study of a TCE later acquired by Ouro Medicines. No
such study of Ouro's molecule, CM336, is on ClinicalTrials.gov, and the
Chinese registries were not searched. Cizutamig, the molecule that does
have a registered volunteer study, is also a Chinese-origin BCMA x CD3
engager, and the two may have been conflated. Section 2 has both. The
question to put back to the colleague is the trial identifier.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. The Idea

Dose healthy volunteers once or twice each, climbing between cohorts,
and stop at the first dose that either produces a grade 1 cytokine
release syndrome (CRS), which in a volunteer means a fever, or depletes
peripheral B cells by 50%. Call that the active dose, and open the
patient study with a starting dose and step-up regimen anchored to it.

The claim to test is speed. A phase 1 unit recruits from a standing
pool, doses the next cohort within days of the previous readout, and
reads a single-dose cytokine and B-cell response inside a week. A
conventional oncology escalation waits on accrual of patients with the
right disease at the right stage, a 28-day dose-limiting toxicity (DLT)
window, and a cohort review. If the volunteer ladder climbs three times
faster, the gap between the starting dose and the active dose is
crossed before the first patient is enrolled.

## 2. Studies Found

### Registered Healthy Volunteer Studies of T-Cell Engagers

| Study | Molecule | Target | Design | Volunteers | Start | Status | Marker |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| [NCT07236411](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07236411) | Cizutamig (Candid; EMB-06, EpimAb) | BCMA x CD3, 2+2 FIT-Ig | Randomized, double-blind, single IV or SC dose against placebo; absolute bioavailability | 24 healthy adults, all arms | 2025-12-04 | Completed 2026-07-14, no results posted | ❌ |
| [NCT07284797](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07284797) | XmAb657 (Xencor) | CD19 x CD3, 2+1, extended half-life | Open-label first-in-human dose escalation, SC | Healthy adults as the first cohort, then myositis, systemic sclerosis, Sjögren's | 2026-02-24 | Recruiting; primary completion Oct 2028 | ❌ |
| [NCT07712939](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07712939) | CND319 (Candid) | CD19/CD20 x CD3 | Open-label first-in-human; single ascending dose in volunteers, multiple ascending dose in patients | Healthy adults 18–65 in Part 1 SAD; rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren's in MAD and expansion | 2026-07-20 | Recruiting; primary completion Mar 2028 | ❌ |

: T-cell engagers with a registered healthy volunteer cohort, ClinicalTrials.gov, searched 2026-09-10 {tbl-colwidths="[11,14,12,20,17,8,12,6]"}

All three studies started in or after December 2025, all are for
autoimmune indications, and none is an oncology TCE. All three molecules
were engineered for the setting: a CD3 arm with reduced affinity, a long
half-life, subcutaneous administration, and a single dose or short
course as the intended regimen.

**No registry record shows the readout the idea depends on.** The
registered primary outcomes are adverse events (XmAb657, CND319) and
absolute bioavailability (cizutamig), and the secondary outcomes are
serum concentration and anti-drug antibodies. B-cell counts and
cytokines will have been measured but are not registered endpoints, so
what the volunteer cohorts found will have to come from a presentation.
Xencor expects to report on the XmAb657 study in the second half of
2026.

### What Is Known About the Molecules From Patients

**Cizutamig was dosed in volunteers after its dose range was known from
patients.** Before the volunteer study it had been given to 40 patients
with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma at weekly doses of 0.2 to
300 mg, with CRS at grade 1 in 18% and grade 2 in 8%, median onset one
day, and no immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome
(ICANS); and to one patient with refractory rheumatoid arthritis, with
no cytokine release (entry 24). By January 2026 the sponsor reported 80
patients dosed, half with autoimmune disease, mild cytokine release in
fewer than 20%, and no ICANS. That order is the reverse of the idea in
Section 1. The study measured bioavailability, and it shows that a
volunteer can be dosed, not that the active dose was found that way.

**XmAb657 matches the idea:** a first-in-human escalation whose first
cohort is healthy participants. In cynomolgus monkeys a single dose
held B cells below 5 cells/µL for at least 42 days, in lymph node and
marrow as well as blood, with no clinical signs of cytokine release and
a half-life near 15 days (entry 25). The registry record does not say
whether the volunteer cohort climbs to a B-cell-depleting dose or stops
at a dose chosen to be subactive. That is the first thing to find out
when the study reports.

### The Ouro Medicines Molecule

CM336 (gamgertamig) is a BCMA x CD3 engager developed by Keymed
Biosciences in Chengdu. It has been in a phase 1/2 in multiple myeloma
in China since 2022, and in autoimmune cytopenias, bullous disease,
Sjögren's and several plasma cell disorders since 2025. Keymed licensed
rights outside Greater China to Platina Medicines, a unit of Ouro
Medicines, in January 2025, and the molecule became OM336. Gilead
announced the acquisition of Ouro in March 2026 and completed it in
June.

The registered OM336 studies are in autoimmune cytopenias (United
States and Australia), Sjögren's and myositis (New Zealand), and
sensitized kidney transplant candidates (Austria and Germany). None
enrols healthy volunteers. The one CM336 record carrying the
healthy-volunteer flag, NCT06745687, is a study in high-risk smouldering
myeloma, and the flag is a registry error.

A Chinese healthy volunteer study of CM336, if one exists, would be on
the Center for Drug Evaluation registry (chinadrugtrials.org.cn) or the
Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, and neither was searched. Cizutamig is
the other candidate for what the colleague recalled: also a
Chinese-origin BCMA x CD3 engager, from EpimAb in Shanghai by way of
Vignette Bio and Candid Therapeutics. Ask the colleague for the trial
identifier or the molecule's code.

### Search Coverage

Searched: ClinicalTrials.gov, by intervention terms (bispecific,
trispecific, T-cell engager, CD3) restricted to studies accepting
healthy volunteers; Europe PMC for published reports of a CD3-engaging
bispecific in healthy subjects, which returned none; and press releases
and meeting abstracts for the three molecules found.

Not searched: the Chinese registries, the EU Clinical Trials register,
the Australian register (ANZCTR), and the PAGE and ACoP abstract
archives.

## 3. What a Volunteer Study Can Measure

The readouts after a single dose, in the order they arrive:

| Hours after dose | Readout | What it says |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 2–6 | Lymphocyte count falls (T-cell margination) | CD3 was engaged. The earliest pharmacodynamic signal, present at doses well below the active one. |
| 2–24 | IL-6, IFN-γ, TNF in serum | How strongly T cells were activated. A grade 1 CRS is the clinical sign of the same process. |
| 6–48 | Fever | Grade 1 CRS, the first of the two stopping signals in Section 1. |
| 24–72 | Peripheral CD19+ B cells | Depletion, the second stopping signal: depth at nadir and, on later visits, duration. |
| Days to weeks | Serum concentration, anti-drug antibodies | PK, and whether a second dose can be interpreted. |

: Single-dose readouts in a healthy volunteer, and what each one answers {tbl-colwidths="[14,32,54]"}

**The two stopping signals will not arrive together.** A CD3 arm tuned
down, as in all three molecules in Section 2, is tuned to deplete
without releasing cytokine. In a volunteer, B cells may fall by half or
to zero at a dose that produces no fever, and the first fever may come
a log higher or never. The idea as posed treats either signal as
"active", so the design has to choose, because the two name different
doses. For an autoimmune programme the answer is depletion, since
depletion is the goal and fever the cost. The fever dose then becomes an
upper bound the patient study need not approach.

**Several volunteers per dose.** Volunteers are not scarce, so there is
no reason for one person to climb the ladder. A cohort of four to six
per dose level, with a sentinel pair dosed a day ahead of the rest, is
the ordinary phase 1 shape, and it estimates the between-subject
response at each dose, which one person climbing cannot.

**A second dose in the same volunteer measures tolerance.** Give a
priming dose, wait a week, give a higher dose, and compare the cytokine
response with a cohort that received the higher dose without priming.
That measures the tolerance effect, a primed T-cell pool releasing less
cytokine at the next dose, in a system with no tumour and no disease,
and a step-up regimen for patients would be designed from it. The
confound is that by the second dose the volunteer's blood B cells are
gone, so a lower cytokine response could mean primed T cells or a
missing target. Tissue B cells persist longer than blood B cells and
make up most of the pool, so the comparison still informs, but the
B-cell measurement has to separate the two explanations.

## 4. Translation From Volunteer to Patient

A volunteer's active dose is useful to the extent that a patient's
response at the same dose can be predicted from it. Three things differ.

**Target burden.** Cytokine release scales with the number of target
cells the engager finds. A volunteer's peripheral B-cell count is in the
ordinary range, and an autoimmune patient's is usually similar unless
prior rituximab has emptied it; the plasma cell compartment that a BCMA
engager targets is larger in a patient with active humoral disease. A
patient with a haematological malignancy carries orders of magnitude
more target. The volunteer's fever dose is therefore a lower bound on
the fever dose in a low-burden patient, and an overestimate, by an
unknown factor, for a patient with a tumour. The B-cell depletion dose
translates better, since depleting a normal-sized compartment is the
same event in both.

**T-cell fitness.** An autoimmune patient on glucocorticoids,
mycophenolate or methotrexate has a suppressed T-cell response and a
volunteer does not. The volunteer dose may over-predict activity in a
treated patient, so the patient study would start too low rather than
too high: safe, and slow.

**Duration.** A volunteer given a long-half-life engager loses
peripheral B cells for weeks to months (42 days or more in the primate
study, entry 25). The volunteer bears that cost for no benefit, which is
why all three registered studies are for indications where a single
administration is the intended regimen. The ethics review will have
weighed it and the consent form will say how; neither document has been
read.

**The translation holds** for autoimmune indications, B-cell or
plasma-cell targets, engineered CD3 arms, and a depletion readout rather
than a fever readout. Those are the conditions the three registered
studies were run under, and the conditions under which the idea in
Section 1 works. Outside them, the volunteer dose is a minimal
anticipated biological effect level (MABEL) with human data behind it,
which still improves on a MABEL without.

## 5. Where It Applies, and How Much Time It Saves

A volunteer study replaces a prediction of the active dose from primate
data with a measurement in humans. What remains uncertain is the
volunteer-to-patient translation of Section 4, a factor of a few rather
than of tens.

- ✅ **B-cell-depleting TCE, autoimmune indication.** Run the volunteer
  study. Start the patient study one or two steps below the volunteer
  depletion dose, with a step-up regimen designed from the volunteer
  cytokine data.
- ❌ **Solid-tumour or haematological TCE.** No volunteer has been dosed
  with an oncology TCE, the target-burden argument in Section 4 says a
  volunteer readout would not translate, and depleting a healthy
  person's B cells for a lymphoma programme is harder to justify than
  for an autoimmune one.

The time saving below rests on assumptions, not measurements, and each
row is there to be replaced.

| Quantity | Conventional 3+3 in patients | Volunteer single ascending dose |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Recruitment per cohort | Weeks, disease-dependent | Days, from a standing pool |
| Observation before the dose decision | 28-day DLT window | 7 days: CRS window closed, B-cell nadir passed |
| Cohort cadence | 6–8 weeks | 1–2 weeks |
| Dose levels to cross a 3-log gap at 3x steps | 6–7 | 6–7 |
| Time to the active dose | 9–14 months | 2–4 months |

: The speed claim, under stated assumptions. Both columns cross the same gap; the difference is the cadence. {tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

**The saving is six months to a year.** A saving under about eight
weeks, one conventional cohort cycle plus its accrual, would sit inside
the noise of ordinary trial execution. This one does not, if the cadence
assumptions hold, so check the cadence row first against a real unit's
calendar.

## 6. Next Steps

1. Ask the colleague for the trial identifier behind the Ouro
   recollection, and search the Chinese registries if it does not come.
2. Watch for the XmAb657 volunteer cohort results, expected in the
   second half of 2026. The dose the volunteers reached, what their B
   cells did, and whether anyone had a fever answer most of Section 3.
3. Read entry 20, the EMA first-in-human guideline, for what it says
   about healthy volunteers and immunomodulators, since an ethics
   committee reads that document.
4. Set the speed table against a real phase 1 unit's cohort calendar
   and a real programme's escalation history, so both columns become
   measurements.
